ann_34.text: This part acts on 165 of 242 training patients (68%), nearly all of them patients without chest pain on exercise; 51 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 54-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain and no chest pain on exercise, predicted risk about 3%), it slightly lowers the predicted risk (on the training data only).

Through it, being a woman clearly lowers the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain (for a typical patient, from about 29% to about 1%, against about 33% to about 10% with chest pain on exercise).
Fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL clearly lowers the predicted risk here, and even more so without chest pain on exercise (from about 29% to about 3%, against almost no change with it).
Being a woman also lowers the predicted risk more if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL (on the training data only).

ann_36.text: This part adds to the predicted risk only once serum cholesterol rises above about 285 mg/dL (7.4 mmol/L), and only slightly; across patients the rise above that point happens in an uneven way (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).
It acts on 9 of 242 training patients (4%), and 1 of them had heart disease.

ann_37.text: Through this part, higher resting blood pressure raises the predicted risk steadily, from about 22% at 110 mm Hg to about 40% at 155 mm Hg for a typical patient (on the training data only).

Through the same part, higher cholesterol lowers it in an uneven way across patients, from about 34% at 193 mg/dL to about 24% at 308 mg/dL, offsetting part of cholesterol's overall rise (on the training data only).

ann_38.text: This part acts on 118 of 242 training patients (49%); for the typical patient it acts on it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 3% to about 2% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 23 of these 118 patients had heart disease.

Through it, cholesterol raises the predicted risk steadily up to about 258 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L), then no further, for patients with fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less; this holds for most of them, but for women and patients without chest pain on exercise it changes in stages (on the training data only).

For men, the change happens in a step, mainly the first vessel: going from 0 to 1 vessel coloured adds to the predicted risk here, and more vessels add nothing further through this part (on the training data only).

More vessels coloured raise the predicted risk, in an uneven way across patients, even more so if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL: for a typical patient from about 3% to about 92%, against about 29% to about 98% otherwise (on the training data only).
Through it, being a woman or having fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lowers a typical patient's predicted risk (to about 11% and about 13%) (on the training data only).

ann_39.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has typical angina (about 2%) or non-anginal chest pain (about 4%), and a lower one with atypical angina (about 18%), than with no chest pain symptoms (about 29%).

Each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same for most patients, but for patients without chest pain on exercise the rise levels off: a typical patient goes from about 29% at 0 vessels to about 98% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top (on the training data only).
A flat rather than upsloping ST segment at peak exercise raises it to about 87%, and a reversible defect on the thallium scan to about 52% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise (about 23% at 0 mm to about 52% at 2.8 mm) and higher resting blood pressure (about 22% at 110 mm Hg to about 40% at 155 mm Hg) raise the predicted risk steadily; higher cholesterol raises it in an uneven way, from about 14% at 193 mg/dL to about 50% at 308 mg/dL (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 29% to about 1%, and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lowers it to about 3% (on the training data only).
A higher maximum heart rate lowers the predicted risk steadily, from about 38% at 118 to about 24% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).
Older age raises it steadily but only slightly, from about 27% at 42 to about 32% at 66 years, and chest pain brought on by exercise raises it slightly, by about 4 points (on the training data only).

The model has little data on three categories it treats strongly: a fixed defect on the thallium scan (15 patients; predicted risk about 11% instead of 29%), a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; about 55%) and an ST-T wave abnormality on the resting ECG (2 patients; about 77%), all on the training data only.

ann_34.original: Node 155_a computes a 'benign profile' gate: 155_a = ReLU(0.824*sex:0 + 1.109*exang:0 - 0.509*fbs:0 + 0.088). Activates for female patients (sex:0=1) with no exertional angina (exang:0=1); normal fasting glucose slightly attenuates. Output-facing copy of hidden node 155. Activation profile: active 70% / hard-zero 30% (verified). Reads out to output with weight -0.960, lowering predicted risk. Ablation: removing this readout drops test AUC 0.897->0.869 (-0.028) - the single largest nonlinear contribution to generalisation.
ann_34.proposed: A part that acts on most patients without chest pain on exercise; through it, being a woman and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lower the predicted risk, more so without chest pain on exercise.

ann_36.original: Node 3040 = ReLU(1.052*chol - 0.864): a one-sided cholesterol threshold. Since cholesterol is z-normalised, this turns on only above ~0.82 SD above the mean. Activation profile: hard-zero 82.5% / active 17.5% (verified) - a sparse threshold detector. Feeds node 534 with -0.677; net path effect +0.60 per unit (high cholesterol raises predicted risk). This is the sub-unit that lets cholesterol act as a risk factor only above a level rather than linearly - but it sits inside the 534 gate, which the ablation shows contributes nothing on test.
ann_36.proposed: Cholesterol above about 285 mg/dL (7.4 mmol/L) raises the predicted risk slightly; only 9 training patients are that high, and 1 of them had heart disease.

ann_37.original: Subgraph {trestbps, chol_c, 3240, 2379}: a near-linear resting-blood-pressure signal. 3240 = ReLU(0.978*trestbps + 3.4) is always-on (100% active, verified) - a linear pass-through, not a gate. 2379 = ReLU(0.931*3240 - 0.529*chol_c - 0.754) simplifies to ReLU(0.911*trestbps - 0.529*chol_c + 2.41), near-always-on. Reads out to output with +0.364 (higher resting BP raises risk). Ablation: removing this readout drops test AUC 0.897->0.885 (-0.012) - a modest but real generalising contribution.
ann_37.proposed: Higher resting blood pressure raises the predicted risk through this part, while higher cholesterol lowers it.

ann_38.original: Node 534 = ReLU(0.818*[benign_profile_gate_534path] - 0.677*[chol_threshold] - 1.155*ca - 0.592*chol - 0.761): the model's most elaborate unit, a genuine ReLU gate (hard-zero 53.5% verified) composing four risk signals - vessel count (ca), a cholesterol copy, the cholesterol threshold (3040), and the redundant benign-profile copy (155_b). Net per-unit output effects: ca +1.02, chol +0.52, chol_threshold +0.60, benign -0.72; when the benign signal is strong the whole block is clipped off together. KEY ABLATION RESULT: disabling 534's readout changes test AUC only 0.897->0.899 (+0.002) while train drops 0.946->0.942 - i.e. this showpiece unit is essentially train-only and does not generalise. Signs match cardiology but the structure is fit to the 242 training cases.
ann_38.proposed: A part that acts on about half the patients; through it, cholesterol adds risk only up to about 258 mg/dL, and for men vessels add risk only from 0 to 1.

ann_39.original: Root: y0 = ReLU(bias 0.318 + linear core + 3 nonlinear pathways). (1) DIRECT LINEAR CORE of 17 inputs to the output - ca (largest, +2.03), cp:4 (+1.21), slope:2, chol, cp:2, oldpeak push risk up; sex:0 (-0.71), slope:1, thalach push down. By SHAP the top drivers are ca, cp:4, sex:0, slope:2, chol. (2) benign_profile_gate (155_a, -0.96) lowers risk for females without exertional angina. (3) restbp_chol_interaction (2379, +0.364). (4) risk_aggregation_gate (534, -0.884), the elaborate composed unit. 7 features unused. PERFORMANCE: train AUC 0.946 / test 0.897. ABLATION LADDER (test AUC, baseline 0.897): linear-core only 0.860 (nonlinearity buys +0.037); remove benign gate -0.028; remove restbp -0.012; remove 534 gate +0.002. So the two simple gates (benign, restbp) carry all the generalising benefit; the elaborate 534 aggregation gate is train-only. The benign signal is redundantly encoded twice (155_a direct + 155_b inside 534).
ann_39.proposed: Typical, atypical or non-anginal chest pain lower the predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms. More vessels coloured, a flat ST segment, higher cholesterol, more ST depression, a reversible thallium defect and higher resting blood pressure raise it; being a woman, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL and a higher maximum heart rate lower it.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has typical angina (about 2%) or non-anginal chest pain (about 4%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 29%).

Being a woman lowers the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: for a typical patient it clearly falls from about 29% to about 1% without chest pain on exercise, and from about 33% to about 10% with it.

Each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same to the model's score for most patients, but for patients without chest pain on exercise the rise levels off: for a typical patient the predicted risk goes from about 29% at 0 vessels to about 98% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise raises the predicted risk steadily, from about 23% at 0 mm to about 52% at 2.8 mm for a typical patient; higher cholesterol raises it too, but in an uneven way that differs between patients (from about 14% at 193 mg/dL to about 50% at 308 mg/dL) (on the training data only).

Fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lowers the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: for a typical patient it clearly falls from about 29% to about 3% without chest pain on exercise, but stays at about 32% to 33% with it.
